States the research question and dataset scope (146,028 dyads, four leagues, 2012-13 season).

spans.assertion: dark-skinned players have a statistically significantly higher probability of receiving red cards than light-skinned players, even after adjusting for confounders
the primary adjusted risk difference is 0.24 percentage points (95% CI 0.05 to 0.43, p=0.013) — dark-skinned players have a 0.24pp higher probability of a red card, controlling for all covariates
the secondary adjusted odds ratio is 1.22 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.43) — dark-skinned players have 22% higher odds of a red card
the effect is consistent across multiple model specifications
the effect is robust to various sensitivity analyses
the adjusted risk difference estimate is 0.2405 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0500, 0.4311], p=0.0134, SE=0.000972

after adjusting for games, player characteristics, league country, and referee bias measures, dark-skinned players have a 0.24pp higher probability of a red card, and the CI excludes zero indicating significance at α=0.05
the baseline red card rate for light-skinned players is about 1.23%, so the 0.24pp difference is roughly a 20% relative increase
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.2193, 95% CI [1.0424, 1.4263], p=0.0132
the odds of a red card are 22% higher for dark-skinned players after adjustment, and the CI excludes 1.0 confirming significance
the unit of analysis was a player-referee dyad aggregating all encounters over a player's career, with the outcome being whether any red card was ever received from that referee

the complete-case sample comprised 104,972 dyads (89,019 light-skinned [84.8%], 15,953 dark-skinned [15.2%]) with 1,322 total red cards (1,097 among light-skinned [1.23%], 225 among dark-skinned [1.41%])
skin tone was measured by two independent raters, blind to the research question, rating players from profile photos on a 5-point scale from 0.00 (very light) to 1.00 (very dark)
players were classified as light skin (mean rating 0.00-0.375) or dark skin (0.75-1.00) for the primary analysis, with medium-skin players (0.375-0.625) excluded to maximize contrast
inter-rater agreement between the two skin-tone raters was strong (correlation > 0.85)

the fully adjusted logistic regression model included as covariates: number of games in the dyad, player age/height/weight/position, league country, and referee-country implicit and explicit bias scores

each covariate was chosen for a stated rationale: games for exposure, player characteristics for physical/style confounding, position for foul-rate differences, league for refereeing-standard differences, and bias measures for country-level racial attitudes
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded because player photos were unavailable or unratable for skin tone
11,406 dyads (7.8%) with medium skin tone were excluded from the primary analysis to maximize contrast
8,243 dyads (5.6%) were excluded for missing covariates (7,628 missing position, 46 missing height, 686 missing weight, 132 missing bias measures)
total exclusions amounted to 28.1% of the original dataset (41,056 of 146,028 dyads)

a descriptive comparison found the excluded medium-skin-tone group had a red card rate (1.23%) identical to the light-skin group (1.23%), taken to suggest the medium-skin exclusion does not introduce bias
missing photo data is speculated to be more common among bench players with less exposure, which is suggested to bias the exclusion in a conservative direction
the outcome variable was dichotomized as any red card (1) vs. no red card (0) in the dyad
skin tone ratings from the two raters were averaged into a single score
the averaged skin tone score was categorized into light/medium/dark groups
player age was calculated from birth year relative to the 2012 season
player position was simplified from 12 detailed positions into 4 broad categories
no transformations were applied to the continuous covariates (games, age, height, weight)
diagnostics showed acceptable model fit for the untransformed continuous covariates
the model was fit as a logistic regression using maximum likelihood estimation
robust standard errors (statsmodels default) were used
the risk difference was estimated via average marginal effects, averaging the discrete predicted-probability difference across observations
confidence intervals were computed as Wald-type 95% CIs based on the normal approximation
p-values were computed via two-sided Wald tests
no weighting or clustering was used; each dyad was treated as an independent observation

spans.note: Caveat that SEs may be underestimated due to lack of clustering, with a claim that sample size/significance offer 'some cushion'.

spans.assertion: the hypothesis is concluded to be supported: referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players
the adjusted risk difference is statistically significant (p=0.013), below the α=0.05 threshold
